p98: 98.  Accordingly, the Grand Chamber sees no reason to depart from the Chamber’s decision to dismiss the Government’s objection of lack of jurisdiction ratione temporis.
p99: 99.  The Chamber first found that the offences for which the applicant had been tried in the first and second sets of proceedings were the same. Leaving open the question whether the decision granting the applicant amnesty could be regarded as a final acquittal or conviction for the purposes of Article 4 of Protocol No. 7, it went on to examine the merits of the complaint in the light of the exceptions provided for in paragraph 2 of Article 4 of Protocol No. 7. It agreed with the Supreme Court’s conclusion that the General Amnesty Act had been wrongly applied in the applicant’s case, and found that the granting of an amnesty to the applicant in respect of acts amounting to war crimes had constituted a “fundamental defect” in the proceedings, thus opening up the possibility of a retrial.
p100: 100.  The applicant alleged that the offences at issue in the two sets of criminal proceedings against him had the same factual basis and that the classification of the offences as war crimes in the second set of proceedings did not alter the fact that the charges were in substance identical.
p101: 101.  He further submitted that a decision granting an amnesty to an accused must be regarded as a final decision precluding any retrial.
p102: 102. In their written observations, the Government submitted that in the first proceedings the Osijek County Court had applied the Amnesty Act without establishing the facts of the case and without ruling on the applicant’s guilt. In their view, the decision thus adopted did not answer the question whether the applicant had committed the crimes of which he stood accused, nor did it contain an assessment of the charges listed in the indictment. In paragraph 33 of their observations, the Government inferred from this that the decision did not have the force of res judicata. However, they subsequently stated (in paragraph 37 of the same observations) that it satisfied all the criteria of res judicata and could therefore be regarded as a final acquittal or conviction within the meaning of Article 4 of Protocol No. 7.
p103: 103.  Relying largely on the Chamber’s findings, the Government added that no amnesty could be granted in respect of war crimes, and that the granting of an amnesty in the present case had therefore tainted the proceedings with a fundamental defect.
p104: 104.  The Government stated that it had become apparent after the first proceedings had been discontinued that the victims had been arrested and tortured before being killed. Those new elements were sufficient to classify the acts in question as war crimes against the civilian population rather than “ordinary” murders.
p105: 105.  The Government explained that the Croatian State had enacted the General Amnesty Act in order to comply with its international obligations under the Agreement on Normalisation of Relations between the Republic of Croatia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia (23 August 1996), and that the main aim of the Act had been to promote reconciliation within Croatian society at a time when the war was still ongoing. In the Government’s submission, the Act explicitly excluded war crimes from its scope.
p106: 106.  In the present case, the General Amnesty Act had been applied in a manner contrary to its very purpose and in breach of Croatia’s international obligations, in particular those arising under Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention.
p107: 107.  As to the procedures followed by the national authorities, the Government submitted that the applicant’s trial had been fair, without putting forward any argument as to whether the proceedings had been conducted in accordance with the rules of the Croatian Code of Criminal Procedure.
